name: Emulsion
statement: Beat oil into water hard enough, with a binder, and the two unmixable liquids hold together.
statementAccent: the two unmixable liquids hold together
meaning: An emulsion is a mixture of two or more liquids that are normally immiscible, unable to mix, such as oil and water, in which one liquid is dispersed as tiny droplets throughout the other. The droplets form the dispersed phase, and the surrounding liquid is the continuous phase. Emulsions come in two main types: oil-in-water, where oil droplets float in water, as in milk, mayonnaise, and vinaigrette, and water-in-oil, where water droplets sit in fat, as in butter and margarine. Because oil and water naturally separate, emulsions are inherently unstable and require energy, such as whisking or homogenizing, to break one liquid into droplets, and usually an emulsifier to keep them from recombining. Emulsifiers are molecules with a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail that sit at the boundary between the two liquids and stabilize the droplets. Emulsions are ubiquitous in food, from mayonnaise and hollandaise to milk and cream, and the principle extends far beyond the kitchen into cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and industry.
mechanism: Oil and water do not mix because their molecules are chemically incompatible, so left alone they separate to minimize contact. To make an emulsion, mechanical energy, from whisking, blending, or homogenizing, is used to tear one liquid into tiny droplets and disperse them through the other. But such a mixture is thermodynamically unstable and tends to separate again, through creaming, where droplets rise or settle, and coalescence, where droplets merge back together. An emulsifier stabilizes it. Emulsifiers are amphiphilic molecules, with a hydrophilic, water-loving head and a hydrophobic, oil-loving tail; they position themselves at the oil-water interface, their heads in the water and tails in the oil, lowering the interfacial tension and coating each droplet so the droplets repel rather than merge. Lecithin, abundant in egg yolk, is a classic food emulsifier, and mustard is another. This is why mayonnaise, an oil-in-water emulsion of a great deal of oil dispersed in a little water and vinegar, holds together, stabilized by the lecithin in egg yolk.

examples.text: Mayonnaise is an oil-in-water emulsion in which a large amount of oil is dispersed in water and vinegar, stabilized by egg yolk lecithin.
Butter and margarine are water-in-oil emulsions, with water droplets dispersed through fat, the reverse of milk and mayonnaise.
A whisked vinaigrette is a temporary emulsion that soon separates, since it lacks a strong emulsifier to keep oil and vinegar combined.

variants.name: Oil-in-water versus water-in-oil
variants.text: The two basic types: oil droplets in water, as in milk and mayonnaise, versus water droplets in fat, as in butter.

variants.name: Emulsifiers
variants.text: Amphiphilic molecules like egg-yolk lecithin that sit at the oil-water interface and stabilize the droplets against separation.

whyItMatters: Emulsions are fundamental to cooking and to countless products, letting oil and water, which naturally refuse to mix, be combined into stable, useful mixtures with desirable textures. In the kitchen they underlie mayonnaise, hollandaise, vinaigrettes, cream sauces, butter, and milk, and mastering emulsification is central to sauce-making and much of cuisine. Beyond food, the same principles govern cosmetics like lotions and creams, pharmaceuticals, paints, and many industrial products, wherever immiscible liquids must be blended. Understanding emulsions explains why sauces break and how to fix them, why an emulsifier like egg yolk or mustard is needed, and how homogenization keeps milk from separating. The concepts of dispersed and continuous phases, emulsifiers, and instability connect everyday cooking to surface chemistry and the behaviour of interfaces.

working.text: use whisking, blending, or homogenizing to break one liquid into tiny droplets dispersed through the other.
include an amphiphilic emulsifier like egg-yolk lecithin to sit at the interface and coat the droplets.
let the emulsifier lower interfacial tension and keep droplets from creaming or coalescing back into layers.

limits: Emulsions are thermodynamically unstable, so even well-made ones can separate over time through creaming or coalescence unless properly stabilized, and temporary emulsions like a simple vinaigrette break quickly. Forming an emulsion requires energy input and, for stability, usually an emulsifier, so oil and water do not combine on their own. The type of emulsion, oil-in-water or water-in-oil, and its stability depend on the proportions, the emulsifier, temperature, and how it is made, and emulsions can invert or break if these change. Classifying a mixture like mayonnaise as oil-in-water can seem counterintuitive given its high oil content, but the water remains the continuous phase.
misreadings: An emulsion does not make oil and water truly mix at the molecular level; it disperses one as droplets in the other, and the mixture is inherently unstable. It does not form on its own, since it needs energy to create and usually an emulsifier to stay together. And a high oil content does not make mayonnaise a water-in-oil emulsion, since its water remains the continuous phase, so treating an emulsion as a true solution, as self-forming, or as classified by which liquid is more abundant, misreads a dispersion of immiscible droplets stabilized against separation.
origin: A basic concept of physical chemistry and food science: a dispersion of one immiscible liquid as droplets in another, stabilized by emulsifiers, underlying many foods and products.
